content.title: Peer Group Mentoring
content.summary: Peer Group Mentoring pairs participants with experienced CNCF open‑source veterans in small pods to discuss technical, community, career, and certification topics. This inclusive format helps Kubernetes users and operators build networks, gain guidance, and foster diverse participation in the ecosystem.

Peer Group Mentoring allows participants to meet with experienced open source veterans across many CNCF projects. Mentees are paired with 2 – 10 other people in a pod-like setting to explore technical, community, career, and certification questions together.

It shows how to evaluate MCP traffic, tie actions to real user identities via OIDC and RBAC, and achieve auditable, tenant‑isolated compliance for AI workloads on Kubernetes.

As AI agents evolve from experiments to autonomous actors in complex systems, they strain traditional authorization models. How can we empower them while enforcing least privilege and governance?

This session introduces agentgateway, a dataplane powered by kgateway that supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and integrates with CNCF policy engines like Kyverno. content.summary: The session demonstrates how to containerize and operate multi‑agent AI workflows on Kubernetes, mapping architectures to Deployments, Services/Ingress, and ConfigMaps/Secrets, and showcasing A/B testing, cost‑per‑move metrics, OpenTelemetry observability, HPA autoscaling, and secure agent‑to‑agent communication via a service mesh with canary/blue‑green rollouts.

content.description:
At Skyscanner scale, every architecture choice carries cost and ops impact. Running dozens of Kubernetes clusters and >60M req/min, we were stuck with costly, complex east-west NLBs. This talk shows how we rebuilt our network to save millions on AWS while preserving resilience and compliance, and how we balanced cost, performance, and auditability.

Attendees learn the architectural changes, migration steps, performance results, and how to contribute to the ongoing Parquet roadmap.

content.description: Kubernetes is supported by a wide contributor community, and the structures that guide the community can be hard to understand at first. content.summary: The session introduces a novel network observability approach that lets operators understand why packets are allowed or denied by interpreting messages from the Linux kernel through OVS/OVN/OVN‑Kubernetes into the NetObserv GUI. A live demo shows the end‑to‑end flow, helping users troubleshoot complex network policies in Kubernetes clusters.

If your network could speak, what would it tell you?
Kubernetes networking is a tricky beast, and observability tools are crucial to make sure it works as you expect. But even if you see WHAT happens in your network, you still don’t know WHY it happens. Especially if you have a number of network policies in the cluster, it is always difficult to tell why exactly a given connection is allowed or denied.

content.title: Observing Chaos: Real-Time Monitoring of AI-Driven Kubernetes Destruction
content.author: Josh Halley
content.summary: The session demonstrates how reinforcement‑learning agents can autonomously generate increasingly sophisticated chaos in a live Kubernetes cluster, using ViZDoom/KubeDoom to “play” against real workloads. It shows how OpenTelemetry tracing and Cilium network observability can be combined into a real‑time dashboard, teaching operators how to instrument AI workloads, build resilient chaos agents, and monitor their impact with CNCF observability tools.

Traditional chaos engineering uses predefined failures. What if chaos evolved with your system’s resilience?

This session showcases a feedback loop where reinforcement learning agents generate progressively sophisticated chaos in a live Kubernetes cluster. content.author: Malgorzata Widelicka & Lukasz Ogrodowczyk
content.summary: The session delivers a hands‑on playbook for balancing cost and performance in Kubernetes by mastering autoscaling with Karpenter and KEDA, emphasizing observability, FinOps and DORA metrics, and strategies for handling spot instances, GPUs, and scaling to zero.
content.description:
Running cost-effective Kubernetes clusters in the face of unpredictable, resource-hungry workloads is a common battle. High costs, long provisioning times for specialized hardware like GPUs, and the risk of instability from spot instances are frequent frustrations. How can practitioners optimize for both cost and performance without compromising stability?

content.author: Florian Forster
content.summary: The session details GitLab’s journey building Runway, an internal platform that unifies the operation of its massive SaaS offering and thousands of self‑managed installations, highlighting why Cloud Run fell short and how Kubernetes became the common foundation to support both deployment models at scale.
content.description: GitLab faces a unique platform engineering challenge: building an internal platform that serves both gitlab.com (with millions of users worldwide) and thousands of self-managed installations ranging from small teams to large enterprises. This talk shares the journey of building "Runway," GitLab's internal platform, and the architectural decisions required to support this dual deployment model. content.author: Peter ONeill

This model worked when networks were smaller and trust was implicit, but in cloud-native environments it creates excessive privilege, blind spots, and unnecessary risk.

content.title: Why Isn't the Fix in My Container? Tracking CVE Propagation Across 10,000 Projects
content.author: Mor Weinberger
content.summary: The session presents a data‑driven analysis of how CVE fixes propagate (or stall) across the open‑source ecosystem—from upstream projects through package managers and base images to final containers—highlighting weeks‑long exposure windows in Kubernetes workloads. It then offers a practical playbook of automated back‑porting, in‑place image patching (e.g., with Copa), and risk‑based prioritization to dramatically reduce mean‑time‑to‑remediation for container‑based deployments.
content.description:
We analyzed CVE remediation patterns across 10,000 open source projects to uncover a critical problem: vulnerabilities fixed upstream often take weeks or months to reach downstream containers. This lag creates massive security exposure windows in Kubernetes environments.

Attendees learn when multi‑cluster is justified, how to encode placement and failover policies, and how to operate Ray Serve safely across clusters, leaving with reference architecture and ready‑to‑use manifests.
content.description: AI inference at scale faces bursty traffic, uneven GPU supply, regional latency, varied SLO requirements, and occasional cluster or availability zone outages. A single cluster cannot reliably meet all of these demands. This session shares a practical blueprint: use Karmada to orchestrate Kubernetes fleets—policy-based placement, replica spreading, and automated failover—and run Ray Serve-based inference with KubeRay’s RayService. content.title: To Upstream or Not? Why Becoming the Maintainer of Your Dependencies Matters
content.author: Christos Markou
content.summary: The session explains why companies should actively maintain the open‑source projects they depend on, using a concrete OpenTelemetry component that was slated for deprecation. By engaging upstream, the speaker kept the component alive, which later enabled rapid resolution of customer issues, demonstrating the business value of upstream stewardship.
content.description: How much time should we invest in maintaining open-source software we rely on? This dilemma often bothers companies, especially observability vendors that build on OpenTelemetry. In this session, the speaker, an active OpenTelemetry contributor and code owner, will share a story showing why caring about open source dependencies is not just altruism. content.title: Beyond Stateless: Distributed Transactions with Autoscaling and Consistency on Kubernetes
content.author: Jumpei Nishitani
content.summary: The session demonstrates how to achieve strong ACID‑style distributed transactions on Kubernetes by coupling a Paxos‑based transaction monitor with the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, enabling stateless microservices to scale automatically while preserving consistency. Attendees learn concrete design patterns and deployment strategies for building transaction‑heavy, autoscaling‑ready applications.
content.description:
This session presents a practical method for implementing distributed transactions with strong consistency and seamless autoscaling on Kubernetes. By integrating a transaction monitor with the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, we show how stateless business applications can retain ACID properties while scaling efficiently. content.author: Sarthak Aggarwal & Madelyn Olson
content.summary: This session provides a technical deep‑dive into deploying and operating Valkey (a Redis fork) at massive scale on Kubernetes, covering sharding, replication, DNS‑based discovery, operator automation, gossip traffic tuning, and strategies to reduce CPU spikes and failover latency. It equips Kubernetes operators with practical guidance to run highly available, performant in‑memory data stores across hundreds of nodes.
content.description:
As cloud-native platforms become the standard for running distributed systems, the need for horizontally scalable, highly available in-memory datastores has immensely increased. In this session, we'll deep dive how Valkey, an open-source Redis fork, fulfills this demand at a very large scale with Kubernetes.

content.author: Luis Ariza

content.description:

content.description: SIG Security helps the Kubernetes project to keep pesky bugs contained, and to spread the word when they escape! From the OWASP Top Ten and WONTFIX issues, to third-party audit results and CVEs, Kubernetes bugs have many different shapes and lifecycles. content.description: Maintaining a healthy open source project amid competing company interests is hard. content.summary: The session details a real‑world migration from Jenkins to a Kubernetes‑native CI/CD stack built on Tekton for declarative, on‑demand pipelines and ArgoCD for GitOps‑driven continuous delivery, highlighting gains in scalability, resource efficiency, and supply‑chain security. It provides practical lessons for teams looking to modernize their CI/CD workflows to run natively on Kubernetes.
content.description: In this session, we’ll share our journey of evolving from traditional CI/CD with Jenkins to a fully Kubernetes-native workflow using Tekton and ArgoCD. As our systems grew more cloud-native, we needed a solution that ran natively on Kubernetes, embraced declarative pipelines, and integrated seamlessly with Git-based operations. content.author: Frédéric Comte
content.summary: This session presents how the statistical offices of Norway and France modernized their data infrastructures by adopting Kubernetes and the broader cloud‑native ecosystem, detailing their data platform architectures and the jointly created open‑source project Onyxia that empowers data scientists within a CNCF‑aligned environment.
content.description:
The statistical offices of Norway (SSB) and France (Insee) have both chosen to embrace cloud-native technologies to modernize their data infrastructures. In our institutions, most developers are data scientists working outside the IT departments. This brings unique challenges for the platforms they use.

content.author: João Soares & João Azevedo
content.summary: This session presents a real‑world case study of running Apache Spark on Kubernetes, detailing how the Spark Operator and Volcano were used to build a self‑service platform, the discovery of an etcd bottleneck caused by massive SparkApplication CRs, and how the API Aggregation Layer can mitigate storage pressure in large‑scale deployments.

We’ll begin by outlining our use case and approach for building a self-service Spark on Kubernetes platform, highlighting how emerging open-source tools like Volcano and Kubeflow’s Spark Operator served as key building blocks to it. content.title: Beyond the Cloud: Managing Baremetal the Kubernetes Way Using Metal3.io: Sylva Project as a Use-case
content.author: Ádám Rozmán, Nicolas Belouin
content.summary: This session explains how Metal3.io enables declarative provisioning and lifecycle management of bare‑metal servers using the Kubernetes API, covering its components (Baremetal Operator, Ironic, CAPM3) and a real‑world deployment in the Sylva telco‑edge project, showing why operators can manage physical infrastructure the same way they manage cloud workloads.
content.description: As Kubernetes extends beyond cloud environments, managing baremetal infrastructure with the same declarative model has become essential. Metal3.io delivers exactly that—integrating provisioning and lifecycle management of physical servers into the Kubernetes ecosystem. content.title: Emissary-ingress: Version 4 and What Comes Next
content.author: Flynn
content.summary: The session introduces Emissary-ingress version 4, covering its new capabilities as a Kubernetes-native API gateway and ingress controller, and discusses the project's roadmap. It matters to operators and developers because it highlights how the updated controller can streamline self‑service ingress management and informs the community about future enhancements.

It's been a long time coming but Emissary-ingress 4 is out. This is the first new major version in some years for Emissary, one of the first Kubernetes-native, self-service API gateways and ingress controllers, and it comes with a lot of questions about what's next for the project.

content.title: Explore TAG Workloads Foundation: Advancing Cloud Native Execution From Core Runtime To Applications
content.author: Stephen Rust
content.summary: The session introduces the CNCF TAG Workloads Foundation, outlining its mission, scope, early initiatives, and subprojects that aim to define standards and best practices for cloud‑native workload execution environments and their lifecycle management. It explains why robust execution models are critical for Kubernetes users and how the community can contribute to advancing runtime and orchestration capabilities.

content.title: SIG Docs and You: The New Chapter of the Kubernetes API Reference Generator
content.author: Kat Cosgrove, Lavish Pal, Rey Lejano
content.summary: The session walks through recent improvements to the Kubernetes API reference documentation generator—code documentation, error handling, deprecation cleanup, and bug fixes—and shows how automating the config.yaml streamlines generation. It highlights upcoming work and invites contributors to help further automate and maintain the docs pipeline, ensuring the project's documentation stays top‑tier for users and operators.

Writing and maintaining that documentation requires the support of a small army of contributors, but there’s an often unseen part of the documentation workflow that still needs attention: the API reference docs generator. content.title: WG-Batch Updates: What’s New and What Is Next?
content.author: Yuki Iwai
content.summary: The session presents the latest enhancements to the Kubernetes Job API—including managedBy and mutable container resources—alongside JobSet resilience features and the InPlaceRestart strategy for faster recovery of large AI/ML workloads. It also showcases Kueue’s multi‑cluster, fair‑sharing, and topology‑aware scheduling capabilities and outlines the collaborative effort with SIG Scheduling on workload‑aware scheduling to embed batch semantics into the core scheduler.
content.description: Join WG Batch maintainers to explore how Kubernetes is evolving to meet the demands of the AI and HPC era. We will present foundational updates to the Kubernetes Job API, such as the managedBy and Mutable Container Resource features. content.author: Juraci Paixão Kröhling
content.summary: This session dives into the hidden costs of high‑cardinality and redundant telemetry in Kubernetes observability pipelines, showing how unbounded metrics, duplicate attributes, and over‑eager auto‑instrumentation can dramatically inflate cloud bills. Attendees learn practical OpenTelemetry Collector patterns and instrumentation scoring techniques to prune waste, control cardinality, and lower expenses without losing essential visibility.

content.title: The Fourth Pillar Arrives: OpenTelemetry Profiling Alpha in Action
content.author: Felix Geisendörfer
content.summary: This session demonstrates the newly alpha‑stage OpenTelemetry profiling signal, showing how to deploy the eBPF‑based profiler in Kubernetes to pinpoint the exact line of code causing a bug introduced by an LLM‑driven refactor. Attendees learn practical steps for using profiling not only for performance tuning but also for rapid incident root‑cause analysis, and hear what remains before the signal becomes stable.
content.description:
The OpenTelemetry profiling signal has officially reached alpha! Join Profiling SIG members Florian and Felix as they recap the journey to this milestone.

Through a live demo, you'll learn how to use this new signal to troubleshoot an elusive bug introduced by an LLM driven refactoring. We'll show you how to set up the OpenTelemetry eBPF profiler, and explain why profiling is not just for performance optimizations, but also for rapidly root-causing incidents down to the specific line of code.

content.title: Is the Agent in the Room with Us Right Now?
content.author: Nick Rutigliano & Andrew Halaney
content.summary: Netflix shares how it evolved its isolation strategy—from Mesos to Kubernetes—by leveraging advanced security mechanisms (seccomp, AppArmor, Landlock), strict RBAC network policies, user namespaces, and storage isolation to safely run hundreds of thousands of diverse workloads while mitigating noisy‑neighbor and multi‑tenant risks.
content.description:
At Netflix we run hundreds of thousands of workloads every day covering every discipline of engineering from backend, frontend, data, machine learning, to the new age of AI agents. As our compute environment has evolved from a Mesos-based implementation to an increasingly more standard Kubernetes environment, we’ll discuss how our isolation strategies have both changed over time and enabled us to run everything Netflix needs in a safe and reliable manner.

content.title: K8s-sigs NFD × SYLVA: Declarative Image-to-Node Compatibility for Telco Clouds.
content.author: Eduardo Arango Gutierrez
content.summary: This session presents a production field deployment that makes image‑to‑node compatibility declarative for telco and edge clouds by attaching a versioned OCI artifact describing kernel, driver, and hardware requirements to container images, validating nodes with Node Feature Discovery before scheduling, and integrating the checks into admission, scheduling, and CI/CD pipelines. It demonstrates how this approach prevents runtime failures for GPUs, RDMA, and kernel modules, improving reliability and performance across heterogeneous telco‑cloud platforms.

content.title: Kubernetes Autopsy: Live Debugging a Cluster Meltdown
content.author: Sandeep Kanabar, Aditi Gupta, Anshika Gupta
content.summary: This deep‑dive walks through a real‑world cluster catastrophe, reconstructing a memory‑leak‑induced OOMKill that destabilized etcd, corrupted state, and triggered a controller storm that collapsed the control plane. Attendees learn advanced debugging and forensic techniques using kubectl, crictl, etcdctl, and eBPF observability tools to read Kubernetes “black‑box” data, pinpoint root causes, and build preventative runbooks.
content.description:
What happens when a Kubernetes cluster spirals? In this technical deep-dive, we'll reconstruct a real-world cluster catastrophe from the digital crime scene it left behind.

Watch as we perform a live forensic analysis of a cascading failure: a memory leak that triggered an OOMKill, which destabilized etcd, which corrupted state, which triggered a controller storm, which brought down the control plane. content.title: Platform Engineering 2.0: Just-Enough Kubernetes and AI-Native DevOps
content.author: Shweta Vohra
content.summary: The talk demonstrates how platform engineering teams can adopt a lean, AI‑native approach by leveraging lightweight Kubernetes (k3s), the Gateway API, ambient service‑mesh, and AI‑enhanced observability tools such as Kubeflow, Argo and Prometheus to build just‑enough, self‑optimising platforms that deliver business value while avoiding over‑provisioned, static systems.
content.description: Over the past year, I’ve seen first-hand that platform engineering is shifting from building everything to building just enough. As our teams re-architected and revived multiple internal platforms, one truth became clear scale without intelligence is waste. content.title: When Multitenancy Goes Wrong: A Deep Dive Into Kcp’s First CVE
content.author: Marko Mudrinić & Marvin Beckers
content.summary: This session provides a technical deep‑dive into CVE‑2025‑29922, a high‑severity vulnerability in the CNCF sandbox project kcp that broke isolation between virtual workspaces, allowing service‑provider accounts to create and delete resources across tenants. Attendees learn the discovery process, the attack vector, its impact on multitenant environments, and the remediation steps taken to secure kcp users.
